title: Air resistance, water resistance and friction
keyIdea: Air resistance, water resistance and friction are forces that act between a moving object and the air, the water or a surface it rubs against. They always push against the motion, so they slow things down. Air resistance grows with area and speed: a bigger parachute falls more slowly, and a cyclist going twice as fast meets about 4 times the push, so racers tuck down. Water is much thicker than air, so water resistance is far bigger: wading is harder than walking. Friction depends on the surfaces: dry rubber grips a wheel rim well, so brakes work, while water or oil cuts the grip and the bike rolls further. Friction can be useful as well as a nuisance.
familyTip: Drop two sheets of the same paper, one flat and one screwed into a ball, from the same height. Which lands first, and why? Then walk across a swimming pool or a paddling pool and talk about what is pushing back on your legs.

visual.caption: Which force is slowing it down? Drag each card to a box, or tap it and then a box.

items: A boat moving through a lake

lab.caption: Flagship lab: point resisting forces, drop four parachutes, speed up a cyclist, race a marble in air and water, test four brakes.

kid: When something moves, the air, the water or the ground can push back on it. These pushes are air resistance, water resistance and friction. They always push the opposite way to the motion. A cyclist rides forwards, so air resistance pushes her backwards. A skydiver falls down, so air resistance pushes her up.

A parachute works by catching lots of air. In the lab the same toy falls 2 metres. With no canopy it takes 0.64 seconds. With a large canopy it takes 1.58 seconds. A bigger area pushes on more air, so the air pushes back harder.

Speed matters too. When a cyclist goes twice as fast, the air pushes back about 4 times as hard. That is why racing cyclists crouch low. Water is much thicker than air, so water resistance is even bigger. A marble takes almost twice as long to fall 30 centimetres in water as in air.

Friction happens when two surfaces rub. Bike brakes press rubber pads onto the wheel rim, and friction slows the wheel. A wet or oily rim grips less, so the bike rolls further before it stops. Friction can be a nuisance, but without it your shoes would slip and brakes would not work.
adult: Ages 9 to 10. The National Curriculum in England (Year 5 forces) asks pupils to identify the effects of air resistance, water resistance and friction, which act between moving surfaces. Pupils should also see that some mechanisms let a smaller force have a greater effect. Year 3 introduced friction on different surfaces. Here the focus is on what makes each resisting force bigger: area, speed, the fluid, and how well two surfaces grip.

The lab figures come from simple models and are estimates. Drag uses F = ½ρCdAv². The 50 g toy is dropped from 2 m with canopies of 0, 0.03, 0.12 and 0.3 m². The cyclist has a drag area of 0.4 m² sitting up and 0.25 m² tucked. A 16 mm glass marble falls 30 cm, with buoyancy included in water. Stopping distance from 15 km/h uses d = v² ÷ 2μg, with grip from 0.6 (dry rubber) down to 0.1 (oily rim). Quadratic drag gives the 4 times rule for double speed.

Common mistakes. Pupils think resisting forces push in the direction of motion, or confuse air resistance with gravity. They expect a bigger parachute to fall faster because it is heavier, or think speed makes no difference. They believe water only pulls you down and has no resistance, and see friction as always bad or only on rough surfaces. Each slip gets its own message in the lab or challenge.

practice.prompt: A boat moves forwards through a lake. Which way does water resistance push on it?
practice.hint: Resisting forces act against the motion.
practice.explain: The boat moves forwards, so water resistance pushes backwards and slows it.

practice.prompt: A cyclist meets {f} N of air resistance. She doubles her speed, which makes air resistance about 4 times as big. About how many newtons is it now?
practice.hint: Twice the speed gives about 4 times the push.
practice.explain: {f} × 4 = {=4*f} N. Air resistance grows faster than speed.

practice.prompt: Why does a parachute slow a falling toy?
choices: Its big canopy pushes on lots of air, so air resistance is bigger
practice.hint: What does the canopy push against as it falls?
practice.explain: Gravity still pulls just as hard. The canopy's large area meets more air, so the upward air resistance is bigger and the fall is slower.

practice.prompt: A bike stops after {d} m with dry rubber pads. On an oily rim the lab says it rolls 6 times as far. How far is that in metres?
practice.explain: {d} × 6 = {=6*d} m. Oil cuts the friction between pad and rim.

practice.prompt: Which change makes friction between your shoes and the floor smaller?
practice.hint: Which one makes the surfaces slippery?
practice.explain: Oil comes between the surfaces, so they grip less and you slip. Rubber soles and carpet give more grip.

pool.prompt: A skydiver falls downwards. Which way does air resistance act on her?
pool.hint: Find the way she moves, then go the opposite way.
pool.explain: She moves down, so air resistance pushes up. Gravity is the force pulling down.

pool.prompt: Which falls most slowly, all carrying the same toy?
pool.hint: Which one pushes on the most air?
pool.explain: The largest area meets the most air, so it has the most air resistance: 1.58 s in the lab, against 0.64 s with no canopy.

pool.prompt: Why do racing cyclists crouch low over the handlebars?
choices: A smaller front area meets less air resistance
It increases friction with the road
pool.hint: How does the shape facing the air change?
pool.explain: Tucking down shrinks the area facing the air. At 40 km/h the lab's air resistance falls from about 30 N to about 19 N.

pool.prompt: A marble takes {t} tenths of a second to fall in air. In water it takes almost twice as long. About how many tenths is twice {t}?
pool.hint: Water slows it to almost twice the air time, so double it.
pool.explain: {t} × 2 = {=2*t} tenths. Water resistance is much bigger than air resistance.

pool.prompt: Why is it hard to run through the sea?
choices: Water pushes back much harder than air
There is no air in the sea
pool.hint: Compare moving through air and through water.
pool.explain: Water is far thicker than air, so water resistance on your legs is much bigger at the same speed.

pool.prompt: Which is a useful effect of friction?
pool.hint: Which one do we want to happen?
pool.explain: Brakes need friction to slow the wheel. Squeaks and worn soles are friction being a nuisance.

pool.prompt: A wet rim makes rubber brakes grip less. What happens to the stopping distance?
pool.explain: With less friction the bike slows more gently, so it rolls further: about 3.0 m wet, against 1.5 m dry, from 15 km/h.

pool.prompt: A bike stops in {d} m on a dry rim. On a wet rim it rolls twice as far. How many metres is that?
pool.hint: Less grip means less friction, so the stop takes longer.
pool.explain: {d} × 2 = {=2*d} m. Water between pad and rim cuts the friction, as in the lab (1.5 m dry, 3.0 m wet).

pool.prompt: A ball rolls across grass and stops. Which force stopped it?
pool.hint: What acts between the ball and the grass?
pool.explain: Friction between the ball and the grass pushes against the motion until the ball stops.
